factCheck.evidence: Wikipedia (Nickelodeon): charged five cents for admission (a 'nickel', hence the name); Penn State Center for the Book: a nickel bought a seat in a movie theater.

Wikipedia (Nickelodeon) and Penn State Center for the Book: Davis and John P. Harris opened the Nickelodeon on Smithfield Street, Pittsburgh, on June 19, 1905; over 100 more opened in Pittsburgh alone.
Wikipedia (Nickelodeon): 'usually set up in converted storefronts'; Britannica's nickelodeon entry: programs of one or two reels lasting 15 minutes to an hour.
Wikipedia (The Great Train Robbery) and Penn State Center for the Book both place The Great Train Robbery on the programs of Davis and Harris's first Nickelodeon in Pittsburgh.
Wikipedia (Nickelodeon): the number of US nickelodeons doubled between 1907 and 1908 to around 8,000; Britannica's nickelodeon entry: about 10,000 by 1910.

Wikipedia (Nickelodeon): early historians saw nickelodeon audiences as primarily working-class people who could not afford higher ticket prices; Penn State Center for the Book describes Pittsburgh workers priced out of $2 playhouse tickets.
San Francisco Silent Film Festival (Miles brothers essay) and FoundSF: before the exchanges, exhibitors had to purchase films directly from the makers.
San Francisco Silent Film Festival and FoundSF: the Miles brothers set up a film exchange in San Francisco in 1902-03, renting films to exhibitors at one-fourth the purchase price.
Wikipedia (Motion Picture Patents Company): founded in December 1908 and also known as the Edison Trust; members included Edison, Biograph, Vitagraph, Essanay, Selig, Lubin, Kalem and others.
Wikipedia (Motion Picture Patents Company): Eastman Kodak held the patent on raw film stock and joined the trust, restricting production to licensed members.

Wikipedia (Motion Picture Patents Company): a 1915 federal ruling found it an illegal restraint of trade under the Sherman Antitrust Act, and an appellate court officially terminated the company in 1918.
Wikipedia (Hollywood, Los Angeles): the Nestor Film Company set up Hollywood's first studio in October 1911 at 6121 Sunset Boulevard.
Wikipedia (Hollywood, Los Angeles): by 1912 major companies had come west to Los Angeles, which became the capital of the US film industry; Britannica's two articles agree on 1915.

Wikipedia (Cinema of the United States): filmmakers were attracted by a warm, predictable climate with reliable sunlight for year-round outdoor filming; Wikipedia (Hollywood, Los Angeles): favorable weather, diverse terrain and low land prices.

Wikipedia (Motion Picture Patents Company): filmmakers moved to Hollywood because distance from Edison's home base in New Jersey made it harder for the MPPC to enforce its patents.

Wikipedia (Alice Guy-Blaché): hired as Gaumont's secretary in 1894; she made La Fée aux Choux in 1896, though its exact dating is debated; the Gaumont company history also records her as Gaumont's secretary from 1894.

Wikipedia (Alice Guy-Blaché): La Fée aux Choux established her as cinema's first narrative fiction filmmaker; an Encyclopedia.com entry notes some scholars dispute calling it the first fiction film, so the card says 'one of the first'.
Wikipedia (Alice Guy-Blaché): head of production at Gaumont from 1896 to 1906; Gaumont's own history: Léon Gaumont gave her charge of production.
Wikipedia (Alice Guy-Blaché): at Gaumont she experimented with synchronized sound using the Chronophone system.
Wikipedia (Alice Guy-Blaché): after marrying Herbert Blaché in 1907 and moving to the United States, Guy co-founded Solax; Encyclopedia.com: in 1910 she and her husband founded Solax.
Wikipedia (Alice Guy-Blaché): in 1912 they invested in a Fort Lee, New Jersey studio, making her the first woman to own a film studio plant.
Wikipedia (Alice Guy-Blaché): she returned to France in 1922 and made no more films, and was long overlooked; Encyclopedia.com: she remained an unknown pioneer for decades.
Wikipedia (D. W. Griffith): joined Biograph in 1908, directed 48 shorts that year alone and hundreds before leaving the company.

Wikipedia (D. W. Griffith): credits him with developing cross-cutting between parallel stories, drawing on Dickens, rather than inventing it; Porter's 1903 cross-cutting is documented by the National Archives.
Wikipedia (The Birth of a Nation): adapted from Dixon's 1905 novel and play The Clansman; runs up to 193 minutes depending on the print, in two parts with an intermission.

PBS Culture Shock: its groundbreaking camerawork, including close-ups, night photography and tracking shots, 'transforms forever the way films are made'; Wikipedia says it helped pioneer close-ups and fade-outs.

Wikipedia (The Birth of a Nation): the film presents the Klan as a heroic force protecting white women and maintaining white supremacy; PBS Culture Shock describes its vicious stereotyping of Black people.
Wikipedia (The Birth of a Nation): many Black characters were portrayed by white performers in blackface.
Wikipedia (The Birth of a Nation): the NAACP protested at premieres in numerous cities, and the film was banned in three states and several cities.

Wikipedia (The Birth of a Nation): William Joseph Simmons revived the Klan in November 1915; John Hope Franklin judged that without the film the Klan might not have been reborn.

Wikipedia (D. W. Griffith): his indignation at efforts to censor or ban the film motivated him to produce Intolerance the following year.
Wikipedia (Charlie Chaplin): on tour with Fred Karno's company, he signed with Keystone in September 1913.
Wikipedia (Charlie Chaplin): the character debuted in Kid Auto Races at Venice in February 1914; Chaplin described baggy pants, a tight coat, a small hat, large shoes and a small moustache.
Wikipedia (Charlie Chaplin): the Tramp became more gentle and romantic from 1915, and 'the Tramp eating his shoe' in The Gold Rush (1925) is among his most famous sequences.

Wikipedia (United Artists): founded on February 5, 1919, by Chaplin, Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and D. W. Griffith; Wikipedia (Charlie Chaplin): he directed almost every Keystone short he appeared in from 1914.
Wikipedia (Steamboat Bill, Jr. and Buster Keaton): the two-ton facade falls around Keaton, who survives through a single open window with only a few inches of clearance.

Wikipedia (Buster Keaton): from age 3 he performed in the Three Keatons, a knockabout act in which he was tossed across the stage, billed as 'The Little Boy Who Can't Be Damaged'.
Wikipedia (Buster Keaton): his stoic expression earned him the nickname 'The Great Stone Face', and he insisted on performing his own dangerous stunts.
Wikipedia (Buster Keaton): he adopted the deadpan look in vaudeville after noticing that when he laughed, audiences laughed less.
Wikipedia (Buster Keaton): The General, set during the American Civil War, combined physical comedy with an epic locomotive chase.
Wikipedia (Silent film): onscreen intertitles were used to narrate story points, present key dialogue and sometimes comment on the action.

Wikipedia (Silent film): The Last Laugh (1924) succeeded with 'almost no intertitles'. Britannica says it used no intertitles for dialogue or explanation; the card says 'almost' because one title introduces the epilogue.
Wikipedia (Silent film): showings 'almost always featured live music', with pianists, often improvising, in small theaters and organists or orchestras in large city theaters.
Wikipedia (Silent film): showings 'almost always featured live music', with pianists, often improvising, in small theaters and organists or orchestras in large city theaters.
Wikipedia (Silent film): studios supplied cue sheets with the film, with notes about effects and moods; the Library of Congress music guide holds over 1,500 silent film cue sheets.
Wikipedia (Joseph Carl Breil): he composed and arranged the score for D. W. Griffith's The Birth of a Nation (1915).

Wikipedia (Strand Theatre, Manhattan): opened in 1914 in Times Square, believed to be the first lavish movie palace built only to show films; Cinema Treasures gives an original capacity of 2,989 seats.
Wikipedia (The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari): a 1920 German silent film directed by Robert Wiene, in which a hypnotist uses a sleepwalker, Cesare, to commit murders.

Wikipedia (The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari): sets by Hermann Warm, Walter Reimann and Walter Röhrig, with sharp-pointed forms, oblique lines and structures that lean and twist; the main story is framed as a delusional flashback.
Wikipedia (The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari): 'shadows and streaks of light are painted directly onto the sets, further distorting the viewer's sense of perspective'.
Wikipedia (The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari): 'the quintessential work of early German Expressionist cinema', with a major influence on later films.
Wikipedia (Nosferatu): a 1922 German Expressionist film directed by F. W. Murnau, an unauthorized adaptation of Dracula.
Wikipedia (Cinema of the Soviet Union): 'Vladimir Lenin viewed film as the most important medium for educating the masses in the ways, means and successes of communism.'
Wikipedia (Cinema of the Soviet Union): the world's first state filmmaking school was established in Moscow in 1919; Wikipedia (Lev Kuleshov): one of the founders of the world's first film school.
Wikipedia (Cinema of the Soviet Union): the Russian film industry and its infrastructure, including electrical power, had deteriorated to the point of unworkability after the war and revolution.
Open Culture and EBSCO Research Starters: Kuleshov used a print of Intolerance in lessons in which students rearranged its shots in hundreds of combinations.
Wikipedia (Soviet montage theory): the theory holds that editing is the essential element of cinema; the term comes from the French for assembly or editing.

Wikipedia (Soviet montage theory) quotes Eisenstein: 'montage is an idea that arises from the collision of independent shots'; a course reader of his essay 'A Dialectic Approach to Film Form' has the engine comparison.

Wikipedia (Battleship Potemkin): a 1925 Soviet silent film by Eisenstein, made for the 20th anniversary of the 1905 revolution, dramatizing the crew's mutiny against their officers.

Wikipedia (Battleship Potemkin): the Odessa Steps scene, with Cossacks attacking unarmed civilians, is its best-known sequence and a prime example of Soviet montage editing.

The Canadian Encyclopedia: first shown in New York in the summer of 1922, it caused an immediate sensation; Wikipedia: the first feature-length documentary to achieve commercial success.
Wikipedia (Nanook of the North): shot from August 1920 to August 1921 near Inukjuak (Port Harrison), with Allakariallak, a celebrated hunter, as Nanook.
Wikipedia (Nanook of the North): a specially built three-walled igloo was used for the camera and light; the San Francisco Silent Film Festival essay: Flaherty built a "set" igloo.
Wikipedia (Nanook of the North): the women depicted as Nanook's wives were not his wives.
Wikipedia (Nanook of the North): the hunting scenes were deliberately staged using traditional methods.
Wikipedia (Nanook of the North): the hunts were staged with traditional methods rather than the rifles Inuit used at the time, since Flaherty wanted to show life before European contact.
The Canadian Encyclopedia: Flaherty was the first to successfully combine documentary footage with the art of storytelling; Wikipedia: Nanook proved the documentary genre's commercial viability.
Wikipedia (John Grierson): 'In 1926, Grierson coined the term documentary in a review of Robert J. Flaherty's Moana' (New York Sun, February 8, 1926).
